what: Vertical kit: what each piece is for and where it goes. For the agent who builds storeys and roofs. Nothing here is generated or wired yet (2026-10-05).

conventions.units: inches; W = width (across the direction of travel), D = depth / run (the direction a stair climbs), H = height
conventions.stair_rule: Every stair cell rises exactly 60 in, one step of the world's 5-ft height lattice. Full flight = 1x2 cells (10 steps of 12 in x 12 in, 45 degrees); half flight = 1 cell (5 steps). A pawn on the first cell of a flight stands at about +2.5 ft, on the second at about +7.5 ft.
why_1x2_not_1x3: a 1x2 flight is exactly two 5-ft cubes, so the half flight (dais, stage, half level) is literally half of it and the L and dog-leg stairs are made of the same half flights plus a 5-ft landing: one module, not two
at 1x3 a cell rises 3.33 ft, which is on no lattice, and the half flight would be 1.5 cells long
inn and cottage rooms are 4 to 6 cells across: three cells of stair plus a cell of floor at each end is most of a wall
ten 12-in steps read as steps from the top-down camera and survive image-to-3D; fifteen 8-in steps blur into a ramp
the cost is a 45-degree pitch (a real house stair is 35 to 38): acceptable at table distance. The one stair that is looked at, stair-grand, takes 3 cells of run at 8-in risers
conventions.stair_top: The top tread is level with the upper floor (z = 120). The upper slab is cut away over the stair's cells; the cell beyond the top tread is floor.
conventions.stair_width: Treads are 48 in wide, centred in the 60-in cell: 6 in each side for the wall panel's thickness or a railing.
conventions.handed: stair-quarter-turn, stair-wall-hugging and the ladders are right-handed as specified; mirror the mesh for the other hand.
conventions.fit: Pieces marked fit:box must be scaled PER AXIS to their size_in (not uniformly by the largest dimension, which is what the library does today): the image-to-3D generator ignores stated proportions, and a stair that is 8% short does not meet the floor. A per-axis stretch of up to about 15% is invisible on steps; beyond that, regenerate.
conventions.sink: Roof furniture (dormers, chimneys, ridges, finials) has a flat bottom and a plain lower part and is SUNK into the sloping roof plane; nothing is cut to the pitch, so one mesh serves every pitch.
conventions.sparse: Harry: roof furniture 'will be sparse'. Guide: chimneys = one per fireplace stack; dormers = one per attic room or one per bay on a mansion; one weathervane per building; a gargoyle per 15 to 20 ft of parapet; a nest on one roof in three.
conventions.roof_surfaces: See flats.json: four seamless roofing textures with courses along image X and eaves at image bottom.

ladder: ladder-wood--leaning under floor-trapdoor (existing mesh) or roof-hatch
chimney: chimney-stack--* lines up over the fireplace below

pieces.anchor: low end on the -D edge of cell 1 at floor level; top tread at the +D edge of cell 2, level with the upper floor (z=120). Needs a 1x2 opening in the upper floor above the flight (headroom); the cell beyond the top step must be floor
pieces.supersedes: stair-straight--dressed-stone (inn-01: measures 61 w x 110 run x 84 rise, so it climbs 7 ft, not 10)
pieces.use: The default storey stair in stone buildings (castle, crypt, dressed-stone inn). Rises one full storey (120 in) over 2 cells; 45 degrees, 12-in treads and risers. No rail: put it against a wall, or let the engine add railings.

pieces.anchor: as stair-straight--dressed-stone--t10
pieces.supersedes: stair-straight--rough-timber (inn-01: measures 110 x 77 x 94 high, wrong pitch and too wide for a cell)
pieces.use: The default storey stair in timber buildings (inn, cottage, log cabin). Same geometry as the stone one, so the generator can swap them by wall family.

pieces.anchor: low end at the -D edge of its cell, top tread at the +D edge at z=60
pieces.use: Rises 5 ft in one cell: up to a dais, stage or half level (docs/VERTICAL.md: 5-ft half-steps). Half flight + landing + half flight = a dog-leg built from parts.

pieces.anchor: fills its cell; top surface at z=60
pieces.supersedes: stair-landing--dressed-stone (inn-01: only about 35 in high, so it meets no half flight)
pieces.use: A 5-ft-high landing cell, level with the top of a half flight. Turns a stair (dog-leg, U-turn) or extends a mezzanine. The timber one is open underneath (storage, a hiding place); the stone one is solid.

pieces.anchor: upper floor needs an opening over the landing cell and the upper-flight cell
pieces.use: One storey in a room corner, as ONE mesh. Right-hand turn; mirror it for a left-hand turn. Occupies three cells of a 2x2 block: lower flight in cell (0,0) climbing +D, landing in (0,1) at z=60, upper flight in (1,1) climbing +W, arriving at the +W edge at z=120.

pieces.anchor: low end at the -D edge of its cell, top tread at the +D edge at z=60
pieces.use: Rises 5 ft in one cell: up to a dais, stage or half level (docs/VERTICAL.md: 5-ft half-steps). Half flight + landing + half flight = a dog-leg built from parts.

pieces.anchor: fills its cell; top surface at z=60
pieces.supersedes: stair-landing--rough-timber (inn-01: only about 35 in high, so it meets no half flight)
pieces.use: A 5-ft-high landing cell, level with the top of a half flight. Turns a stair (dog-leg, U-turn) or extends a mezzanine. The timber one is open underneath (storage, a hiding place); the stone one is solid.

pieces.anchor: upper floor needs an opening over the landing cell and the upper-flight cell
pieces.use: One storey in a room corner, as ONE mesh. Right-hand turn; mirror it for a left-hand turn. Occupies three cells of a 2x2 block: lower flight in cell (0,0) climbing +D, landing in (0,1) at z=60, upper flight in (1,1) climbing +W, arriving at the +W edge at z=120.

pieces.anchor: as stair-straight--dressed-stone--t10
pieces.use: Castle and dungeon version of the straight flight: runs along a wall with a sheer open side (a fall hazard, catalog aff:hazard). Flat side goes to the wall; mirror for the other hand.

pieces.anchor: centre of the 2x2 block; bottom step and top step both on the -D side; the upper floor is cut away over the whole 2x2 except the arrival cell edge
pieces.use: Tower stair: fills a 2x2 block (9 ft across, a 6-in margin for the tower wall). ONE full turn per storey, so the foot and the head are on the same bearing: copies stack floor on floor and every floor enters on the same side.

pieces.anchor: as stair-spiral-wide--dressed-stone
pieces.use: Timber tower / mill / wizard's-loft stair. Same geometry and stacking rule as the stone spiral.

pieces.anchor: low end at the -D edge of a 2x3 block, top tread at the +D edge at z=120; upper floor open over the upper two rows (2x2)
pieces.use: The mansion foyer's focal piece: 2 cells wide, 3 cells of run (the one stair at a natural 34-degree pitch, because it is looked at, not squeezed in). Arrives at a gallery or upper landing.

pieces.anchor: foot 34 in out from the wall or opening edge, head at z=120 on that edge
pieces.supersedes: ladder-wood (inn-01: plate rated 1 star, 'what's with the jumbo rung?')
pieces.use: Loft, hayloft and roof-hatch ladder: stands in one cell, head resting on the edge of the opening above (a floor-trapdoor or roof-hatch in the same cell). Its top passes 6 in above the upper floor so it shows at the upper cut height.

pieces.anchor: flat against a wall face, foot at floor level, head at z=120
pieces.use: Wall-fixed ladder for shafts, towers, wells and wall-walk access; takes no floor cell (wall edge). Stack copies for taller climbs.

pieces.anchor: on a cell corner or edge midpoint, top at z=108
pieces.use: Carries the outer corner of a jetty, a porch roof or a gallery edge: one storey of wall height (108 in), so the slab or bracket sits on its head. The existing post-timber mesh has arms (it measures 67 in wide); this is the straight one.

pieces.anchor: back face on the outside of the lower wall, top face at z=108 (under the slab), projecting 30 in outward
pieces.use: Under a jettied upper storey: the upper floor oversails the lower wall by 30 in (half a cell). One bracket under each joist end, i.e. at every cell boundary along the jettied side (every 5 ft) and at the corners.

pieces.anchor: as jetty-bracket--s1
pieces.use: Shape variant of the jetty bracket for richer town houses and inns; also under a timber balcony (balcony-wood).

pieces.anchor: flat back on the outside wall face, foot on the ground
pieces.use: Exterior only: against the outside of stone walls of tall rooms (great hall, chapel, crypt above ground), on cell boundaries between windows, one per 10 ft. One storey high; stack two (the upper one scaled 0.8 in depth) for a 20-ft hall.

pieces.anchor: as buttress--s1
pieces.use: Castle curtain walls, barns, old church walls, shored-up ruins. Same placement as buttress--s1.

pieces.anchor: flat back on a wall face, flat top at the underside of what it carries (default mount 90 in = top at z=108)
pieces.use: Under a stone balcony, a projecting parapet or wall-walk (machicolation look), a hall's roof-beam ends, an oriel. In rows at 30-in centres under a parapet, or pairs under a balcony.

pieces.anchor: as corbel-stone--s1
pieces.use: Mansion and temple version: under balcony-stone, mantel shelves, and the eaves cornice of a slate roof.

pieces.anchor: window front parallel to the eaves, centred on a cell, front face 1 to 2 ft up-slope of the wall line
pieces.supersedes: roof-dormer--dressed-stone and --rough-timber for tiled roofs (the inn-01 pair stay as generic fallbacks)
pieces.use: Dormer for clay-tile roofs (town house, better inn). Sink it into the roof plane until the sill is 6 in above the slope; the roof builder clips nothing, the plane simply hides the back.

pieces.anchor: window front parallel to the eaves, centred on a cell, front face 1 to 2 ft up-slope of the wall line
pieces.use: Dormer for thatched roofs (cottage, poor inn): the 'eyebrow' that lifts the thatch over an attic window. Sink it into the roof plane until the sill is 6 in above the slope; the roof builder clips nothing, the plane simply hides the back.

pieces.anchor: window front parallel to the eaves, centred on a cell, front face 1 to 2 ft up-slope of the wall line
pieces.use: Dormer for slate roofs (mansion, town hall); in a regular row, one per bay, aligned over the windows below. Sink it into the roof plane until the sill is 6 in above the slope; the roof builder clips nothing, the plane simply hides the back.

pieces.anchor: window front parallel to the eaves, centred on a cell, front face 1 to 2 ft up-slope of the wall line
pieces.use: Dormer for wood-shingle roofs (lodge, mill, log house); lights a whole attic room. Sink it into the roof plane until the sill is 6 in above the slope; the roof builder clips nothing, the plane simply hides the back.

pieces.anchor: over the hearth; top 3 ft above the ridge if within 5 ft of it
pieces.use: The ordinary town / inn chimney; on tile and shingle roofs. A chimney is a vertical connector (docs/VERTICAL.md): place it straight above the fireplace on the wall below so the two line up through every storey; sink the plain lower shaft into the roof.

pieces.anchor: as chimney-stack--brick
pieces.use: Stone-built houses, castles' domestic ranges, log cabins. A chimney is a vertical connector (docs/VERTICAL.md): place it straight above the fireplace on the wall below so the two line up through every storey; sink the plain lower shaft into the roof.

pieces.anchor: long side parallel to the ridge
pieces.use: Mansion skyline: one per pair of fireplaces, usually on the ridge or at a gable end; the tallest thing on the roof. A chimney is a vertical connector (docs/VERTICAL.md): place it straight above the fireplace on the wall below so the two line up through every storey; sink the plain lower shaft into the roof.

pieces.anchor: on the ridge line
pieces.use: Thatched and peasant roofs: sits low on the ridge. A chimney is a vertical connector (docs/VERTICAL.md): place it straight above the fireplace on the wall below so the two line up through every storey; sink the plain lower shaft into the roof.

pieces.anchor: on a cell edge at roof level (z = top of the wall), outer face flush with the wall face below
pieces.use: The ledge of a flat or low-pitched roof and of a roof terrace: on the roof's cell edges, at the outside face of the wall below. Half cover. Also a terrace edge at ground level.

pieces.anchor: on a cell vertex at roof level
pieces.use: At every corner and free end of a parapet run (the way hedge-end-block ends a hedge). A roof-finial or gargoyle-spout may sit on / under it.

pieces.anchor: on a cell edge at roof / wall-walk level, outer face flush with (or 6 in proud of, on corbel-stone) the wall below
pieces.use: Castle roof and wall-walk edge (three-quarter cover behind the merlon, half behind the crenel). Copies butt into merlon / crenel / merlon at 5-ft rhythm. If the castle designer specifies the same role, keep one sku.

pieces.anchor: on a cell vertex at roof level
pieces.use: At every corner and free end of a battlement run.

pieces.anchor: centred on the ridge line, sunk 4 in
pieces.use: Along the ridge of a thatched roof, end to end. Thatch ridges are the one ridge that really is a raised, sculpted thing, so it is worth a mesh.

pieces.anchor: centred on the ridge line, sunk 2 in
pieces.use: Along the ridge (and hips) of a clay-tile roof, end to end.

pieces.anchor: centred on the ridge line, sunk 1 in
pieces.use: Ridge and hips of slate roofs and (painted the same) of wood-shingle roofs; if the roof code can extrude a ridge roll itself, this mesh is not needed.

pieces.anchor: on a ridge end or gable apex, sunk 3 in
pieces.use: On gable peaks, parapet corner piers and at the ends of a ridge (stone, slate and tile roofs).

pieces.anchor: on a roof apex, skirt sunk over the point
pieces.use: On the apex of a conical or pyramid tower cap (roof-conical), and on dormer peaks.

pieces.anchor: on a ridge end or apex, post sunk 4 in
pieces.use: Roof life: at most one per building, on the highest ridge end or tower apex. May turn slowly in the wind later (the engine can spin it about its post).

pieces.anchor: centred on a cell of the room below, on the roof surface
pieces.use: A vertical connector for thieves and rooftop chases: sits on a flat roof or the ridge-side of a low slope, directly over the room it lights (a mansion stair hall, a studio, a library). Drop through = a 10-ft fall into that room.

pieces.anchor: centred on its cell on the roof / floor surface; the floor below it is open
pieces.use: The way onto a roof, or into a loft from below: placed in the cell over the head of a ladder (ladder-wood--leaning / --upright) or over a stair-spiral-wide top. Closed = floor you can stand on.

pieces.anchor: as roof-hatch--wood
pieces.use: Open state of roof-hatch--wood (two-state swap; align on the Alignment Bench so the curb does not jump).

pieces.anchor: flat back in the outer wall face just below the parapet (default mount 96 in), pointing outward
pieces.use: Sparse: at parapet / battlement corners and gutter ends of temples, castles and old mansions, no more than one per 15 to 20 ft of eaves. Projects outward under the coping.

pieces.anchor: as gargoyle-spout--s1
pieces.use: The everyday version: castles' wall-walk drains, town houses. Same placement as the gargoyle; can be denser (every 10 ft).

pieces.anchor: on any flat-ish roof spot, sunk 1 in
pieces.use: Optional roof life: beside a chimney, in a dormer valley, on a parapet corner pier, on a tower cap. At most one or two per building. (A pigeon is a creature and is left to the creature pipeline.)

existing_library.why: measured 61 x 110 x 84 high (stone) and 110 x 77 x 94 high (timber): neither climbs 10 ft, neither fits a 5-ft cell. New meshes are separate skus with the suffix --t10 (ten-foot storey); the inn-01 meshes stay in place for the rooms that use them.
about 35 in high: meets neither floor nor half level. New 60-in-high landings are separate skus with the suffix --t10.

rise is about equal to run (62-65 w x 110 x 106-113 high): right pitch for this kit. Rescale to 120 rise and it is the outside stair to an upper door. Wider than a cell by a few inches. Not respecified.
by ladder-wood--leaning and --upright (equal rungs demanded in the gate).

the indoor floor-side connector over a ladder (cellar, loft). Measures 18 to 23 in high at a 60-in width, far more than the catalog's 4 in: check whether it is a thick frame or an open lid before placing it flush. roof-hatch is the weathered outdoor one with a curb.
proportions fine (49 x 39 x 60 and 57 x 53 x 60) but their roofing matches none of the four roof surfaces by design; the four material-matched dormers replace them on generated roofs.

existing_library.skus: both (3 stars, note 'is a whole roof')
existing_library.why: each is a complete little roof, not a segment that tiles. Roof planes are code plus the roofing-shingle-wood flat. Keep as a ready-made roof for a 1-cell shed, well-house or porch.

existing_library.skus: --rough-timber (3 stars), --dressed-stone (unrated: 'model isn't bad... specified as outside')
existing_library.why: about 60 x 50 x 50 with its own railing: an exterior piece hung at upper-floor level (bottom at z about 108), over jetty-bracket--s2 or corbel-stone. Harry's note is about placement, which is the generator's job.

catalog says 4 in deep; they measure 30 to 45 in deep at a 60-in length, so they are not a thin edge rail (a base, a return or a diagonal). Look before putting them on stair and gallery edges. No replacement specified: a thin railing is exactly what image-to-3D breaks; a code-made rail (posts + bar) is the better route.

existing_library.skus: both (unrated: 'what is this?', 'not sure what this is supposed to be')
existing_library.why: a gallery is a floor slab at +10 ft with a rail and posts under it: storeys make it (slab + post-timber--plain + rail), no mesh needed.
works as a whole prop at a door (about 110 x 87-100 x 100 high) but carries its own fixed roof; once roofs exist a porch is a lean-to roof plane on two post-timber--plain.
it measures 67 in wide at 108 tall, so it has arms or braces: good in a common room, wrong under a jetty corner. post-timber--plain added.

catalog_lines_to_correct: stair-straight: size 36x110x108 -> 48x120x120 (the kit's flights are specified at this size; the core line is untouched)
stair-grand: fp 2x2, 110x110x108 -> fp 2x3, 120x180x120 (or keep 2x2 and accept a 45-degree grand stair)
ladder-wood: 18x6x120 -> 24x9x120 (chunky), and the leaning one occupies part of a floor cell
roof-thatch / roof-tile-slate / roof-shingle-wood (mesh roof segments): retire in favour of the roofing-* flats when roofs are planes
jetty-overhang (a whole overhanging storey as one kit piece): retire; a jetty is the upper storey offset 30 in plus jetty-bracket
not_specified_on_purpose: stair-spiral in ONE cell (core line; a 5-ft spiral is too tight for 12-in chunky steps)
roof-conical tower cap and roof-gable-end (roof code makes them from the roofing flats)
a U-turn dog-leg as one mesh (build it from stair-half + two stair-landing + stair-half, or use stair-quarter-turn)
